name: Bitter orange (Citrus aurantium, synephrine)
short: Case reports, often multi-ingredient products with caffeine: stroke, ischaemic heart disease, arrhythmia, ischaemic colitis; 5 of 35 left disabled or on medication. Trials: blood pressure rose.
text: A 2023 review of case reports on adverse events related to pre-workout supplements containing synephrine identified 30 reports describing 35 patients with medical complaints after using synephrine-containing supplements; they most often had chest pain, palpitations, fainting and dizziness, common diagnoses were ischaemic heart disease, cardiac arrhythmias and cerebrovascular disease, and five patients were left disabled or remained on medication at last follow-up. The reviewers concluded these supplements may lead to serious adverse health events, while noting that confounding factors such as caffeine could not be excluded. Individual case reports include a 38-year-old man with ischaemic stroke after a week of an "ephedra-free" supplement containing synephrine and caffeine, and a patient who developed ischaemic colitis one week after starting a bitter orange-containing weight-loss supplement and improved when it was stopped. A meta-analysis of placebo-controlled human trials (18 articles) found that systolic and diastolic blood pressure rose significantly with prolonged use (by 6.37 and 4.33 mmHg) and concluded that synephrine tends to raise blood pressure and heart rate. In contrast, in a placebo-controlled crossover trial in 18 healthy adults, bitter orange extract taken by mouth caused no significant changes in heart rate, systolic blood pressure, ECGs or blood tests over the following 8 hours, and no adverse effects were reported. A separate review argues that in the published case reports, which all involved multi-ingredient supplements, the presence of synephrine was never measured and no direct link was demonstrated. No interaction data were found in the cited sources.
